title: Prompt engineering and context engineering
summary: A model call is assembled from instructions, tools, examples, history and retrieved data, and all of it competes for a finite attention budget. Prompt engineering writes the instruction; context engineering decides which tokens are in the window at each step and where they sit. This lesson gives one context-management table (admit, retrieve, defer, clear, compact, note, delegate, order), shows how Anthropic, OpenAI and Google place content for caching, and ends with prompts handled as versioned code behind an evaluation gate. Window sizes, prices and cache numbers live in the LLM fundamentals lesson.

blocks.text: Anthropic documents how its own coding agent manages context. Claude Code compaction passes the message history to the model to summarize, keeps architectural decisions, unresolved bugs and implementation details, drops redundant tool output, and continues with the five most recently accessed files. Project instructions in CLAUDE.md are loaded up front, while glob and grep fetch files just in time.

Anthropic's tool search documentation sizes the problem of tool definitions: as of 2026-10, a typical setup with GitHub, Slack, Sentry, Grafana and Splunk servers can consume about 55k tokens of definitions before work starts, and tool search typically reduces this by over 85 percent by loading only the few tools a request needs.

OpenAI's guidance is to keep production prompts in application code with typed inputs, review and tests. As of 2026-10, OpenAI is deprecating reusable prompt objects in the API and has scheduled the v1/prompts endpoint to shut down on November 30, 2026, so a team that stored prompts on the platform has a migration to plan.

Google's Gemini long-context guide describes a chat-with-your-data app where a user uploads 10 PDFs, a video and some work documents. It says caching the uploaded files and paying to store them is the main optimization there, and puts the cost per request on Gemini Flash at about 4x less than the standard input and output cost (as of 2026-10).

subtopics.title: What fills one call, and who controls each part

blocks.text: Anthropic separates two jobs. Prompt engineering is writing and organizing instructions, above all the system prompt. Context engineering curates the whole set of tokens present at inference, including what lands there outside the prompt: tools, retrieved data, message history. The split matters once a model runs in a loop, because the prompt is written once and the context is rebuilt every turn.

blocks.text: Why not simply use a bigger window? Anthropic's guide and API docs describe context rot: as the token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, so more context is not automatically better. Google's Gemini documentation leans the other way, inviting you to provide all relevant information up front in a window of 1M tokens or more, yet it admits that retrieving many separate facts at once is less accurate than retrieving one (as of 2026-10). The vendors differ in emphasis, so measure on your own cases.

This lesson uses one split from the table. Parts that change at release can be reviewed, versioned and cached; parts that change every call have to be selected. Window sizes, prices and cache numbers are in the LLM fundamentals lesson and are not repeated here.

subtopics.title: Writing the instruction: structure, altitude and examples

blocks.text: A prompt that holds up has distinct sections. Anthropic recommends delimiting them with XML tags or Markdown headers, while noting that exact formatting is likely becoming less important as models improve. OpenAI describes a developer message that usually runs in this order: identity, instructions, examples, then context. OpenAI also uses roles to give instructions different levels of authority: developer messages carry the system's rules and business logic, like a function definition, and user messages carry the inputs those rules are applied to, like arguments to a function.

Anthropic calls the target the right altitude. One failure is hard-coded if-else logic that is brittle and costly to maintain. The other is vague guidance that falsely assumes shared context. The advice is to start with a minimal prompt on the best available model, then add instructions and examples for the failure modes the first tests expose. Minimal is not the same as short: the model still needs enough up front to follow the behaviour you want.

Anthropic calls examples the pictures worth a thousand words. Claude's guidance asks for relevant, diverse examples wrapped in their own tags, and says three to five work best. OpenAI's few-shot advice is the same in spirit: show a diverse range of inputs with the desired output, in place of fine-tuning for a new task. Anthropic adds a warning against stuffing a laundry list of edge cases into the prompt and prefers a small set of canonical examples. Include one example of the hard case, such as the correct reply when the documents lack the answer.

Prompting advice is now model-specific. As of 2026-10, OpenAI says reasoning models give better results from high-level goals while GPT models need precise instructions, and compares them to a senior and a junior colleague. Anthropic's prompting best-practices page opens with a table of per-model guides and says to read the one for your model first, then the general techniques. Copying a prompt from one model to another is a change to be tested, not a free move.

On OpenAI's Responses API the instructions parameter applies only to the current request. If you chain turns with previous_response_id, the instructions from earlier turns are not in the context, so send them again every turn (as of 2026-10).

subtopics.title: Choose the lever before you rewrite the prompt

blocks.text: Anthropic's docs frame prompt engineering as a cycle of test cases, a preliminary prompt, iterative testing and refinement, final validation, then ship. A failing case is evidence, and the first job is to name its class: ignored rule, missing fact, wrong format, weak reasoning or too much noise. Each class points at a different lever. The mapping from symptom to lever is this lesson's convention; the sources cover each lever's own behaviour.

One lever per run. If the prompt and the model id change together and the pass rate moves, you cannot tell which change did it.

subtopics.title: Choosing operations: lossless first, and what you can inspect

blocks.text: Try the rows that choose what enters the window before the rows that remove material. Anthropic calls clearing tool results one of the safest, lightest-touch forms of compaction, and its API docs name server-side compaction the primary strategy for long-running conversations, with context editing kept for finer control. The simplest technique is dropping the oldest turns: Google's long-context guide lists arbitrarily dropping old messages beside summarizing and RAG as what smaller windows often require. It is the cheapest and the lossiest, since nothing records what mattered (this lesson's reasoning).

Anthropic's guide matches the lossy operations to task shapes: compaction for tasks with extensive back-and-forth, notes for iterative development with clear milestones, subagents for complex research where parallel exploration pays. A task can need more than one; Claude Code combines compaction with notes and just-in-time retrieval.

Compaction comes in two beta modes on Claude as of 2026-10. On demand, your application decides when to request the summary. At a token threshold, the API compacts when input tokens reach the trigger you set. The docs say to use on-demand compaction wherever it is available. OpenAI offers a similar pair: server-side compaction with a compact_threshold, and a standalone endpoint for stateless use.

The vendors differ in what you can inspect. Claude's compaction overview lists a third option, your own summarizer, where you own the summarization call, its prompt and the history rewrite, and Anthropic advises tuning that prompt on complex agent traces: maximize recall first, then improve precision. OpenAI's compaction item is encrypted and not meant to be read, so test what survives by asking questions after the compaction (this lesson's advice).

Removal interacts with the cache. On Claude, clearing tool results invalidates the cached prefix, and the clear_at_least setting makes sure enough is cleared each time to be worth it. OpenAI lists its compaction setting among the settings that can prevent reuse from the first changed token onward.
The agent-architectures lesson covers agent-side memory and subagents in depth; here the table stays about one window.

subtopics.title: Assembling a call: what comes first and what comes last

blocks.text: The diagram below lists the parts of one call in the order their tokens sit in the window. The rule behind the order is that whatever is identical between calls goes first, so a cache can reuse it, and whatever changes goes last. In a multi-turn call the history is append-only, so it sits before this turn's documents: last turn's whole call is this turn's prefix. Anthropic and OpenAI state the caching rule in their guidance, and Google's long-context guide puts the question after all other context.

blocks.legend: Read top to bottom: the order of the tokens in one call, an arrow meaning followed by. The Claude cache hierarchy is tools, then system, then messages s5. Breakpoint 1 ends the stable prefix; breakpoint 2 ends the history, which is append-only between compactions, so last turn's cached entry is a prefix of this turn's call s9. Documents and the request change every turn, so they come after it; long documents sit above the query s6. That placement of history is this lesson's reading of s5 and s9. The reply counts toward the window s12, so room is kept for it; window mechanics are in the LLM fundamentals lesson. A layout sketch, not an API trace.

blocks.text: The vendors disagree on where instructions sit relative to long documents. Anthropic's long-context advice puts documents above instructions; OpenAI's developer-message order puts instructions and examples before context. Reading this against the cache rule: on Claude, rules in the system prompt come ahead of messages in the cache order, so documents on top means the top of this turn's user message. This is this lesson's reading; test your layout on your own cases.

A cache breakpoint on content that changes every request writes a new entry each time and never reads one. Anthropic's example is a timestamp inside the prefix. Put the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix, not on the varying block.

Compaction interacts with the cache. OpenAI lists context_management, its compaction setting, among the settings that can prevent reuse from the first changed token onward. What breaks a hit, the lifetimes and the price multipliers are in the LLM fundamentals lesson.

subtopics.title: Prompts as code: versions, pinned models and an eval gate

blocks.text: Treat a prompt as a release artifact. OpenAI's guide says to store production prompts in application code, which gives typed inputs, code review, tests and the normal deployment process, and to roll changes out through feature flags or configuration when you need staged releases. The table lists the controls and the dated fact that decides where a prompt lives on that platform.

blocks.legend: The loop follows the cycle of test cases, prompt, iterate, validate, ship s7; the figure on that page ends with a test against held-out evals. Pinning snapshots, tests and code-managed prompts follow s8. The gate and the split are this lesson's convention. A sketch of the process, not a tool.

blocks.text: The gate needs an evaluation set built to Anthropic's design principles: cases that mirror the real task distribution, edge cases included, graded automatically where possible, with volume preferred over a few hand-graded items. Success criteria should be specific and measurable, such as an F1 floor on a held-out set, not a wish for good performance. Keep part of the set out of the tuning loop and run it only at the gate; the cycle in Anthropic's figure ends with a test against held-out evals. Once a held-out case has decided a release, move it into the tuning set and draw a fresh one, because a case you have seen no longer measures anything new (this lesson's convention). The methods for grading, golden sets and judges belong to the agent-evaluation lesson; this lesson keeps only the loop and the gate.

Two rules make the gate hold. First, a release needs both a pass rate on the held-out cases and no regressions on the tuning cases: a change that lifts the average while breaking a case that used to pass is blocked, and a pass rate measured on the cases you tuned against overstates the result. Second, a model-id change re-runs the full set before the pin moves, and each failure found in production is added to the set, so it tracks the real inputs instead of the ones imagined at design time. Both are this lesson's conventions, applied to the loop in the flow above.

blocks.title: One prompt change behind a gate
items: Write the gate before testing: at least 80 percent of the held-out cases must pass, and no tuning case that passed before may fail.
Build the set from real inputs, awkward ones included: 40 cases in all.
Split it before any tuning: 10 cases go to a held-out set that is run only at the gate, never while editing.
Make one group deliberately hard: 8 of the 40 cases have no answer in the documents, so the right reply is NOT_FOUND.
Run v1 on the tuning cases: 20 pass.
Sort the tuning failures by class. The largest class is an invented answer where the documents had none: 5 cases.
Change one thing: add a rule to reply NOT_FOUND with its reason. Change nothing else.
Run v2 on the tuning cases: 24 pass.
Apply the tuning half of the gate: 1 previously passing case now fails, because a present answer was reported as NOT_FOUND. The release is blocked, and the held-out cases stay unopened.
Change one thing again: add a positive example where the answer sits in the middle of a long document. Run v3 on the tuning cases: 26 pass and no earlier pass has failed.
Run v3 once on the held-out cases: 9 pass, which meets the gate. Release v3 with the model id pinned in the template module and the version tagged in source control.
When the provider ships a new model id, re-run all 40 cases before moving the pin.

blocks.caption: The v3 template and its gate, kept in source control next to the feature. The model id is pinned; the breakpoint ends the stable prefix. This sketch is a single-shot call, so it has no history.
blocks.code:
PROMPT_VERSION = "support-answer@v3"
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"  # Claude model IDs are snapshots; re-run the case set before changing it

RULES = """You are a support analyst for a billing platform.
Answer only from the material inside <documents>.
If the answer is not there, reply exactly NOT_FOUND.
Give the answer inside <answer> tags, one short paragraph.
<examples> ...a few canonical cases, one of them with the answer mid-document... </examples>"""

def build_request(docs: list[str], question: str) -> dict:
    blocks = "\n".join(f'<document index="{i}">\n{d}\n</document>' for i, d in enumerate(docs))
    return {
        "model": MODEL,
        "max_tokens": 1024,
        # stable prefix first; the breakpoint sits at the end of it. It caches only once the prefix
        # reaches the model's minimum length (LLM fundamentals lesson), so the rules and examples must be long enough
        "system": [{"type": "text", "text": RULES, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}],
        # documents above the question, the live request last
        "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"<documents>\n{blocks}\n</documents>\n\nQuestion: {question}"}],
    }

def gate(tuning: list, baseline: dict, held_out: list, threshold: float = 0.8) -> bool:
    regressions = [r.id for r in tuning if not r.ok and baseline.get(r.id)]
    passed = sum(r.ok for r in held_out)
    return not regressions and passed / len(held_out) >= threshold
